So I'm talking about the aggregate level. We have permanent residents. We know how they were listed methodologically speaking, and on the other list we have people who voluntarily registered. So this is the error, the deficiency there. What the Prosecution expert is doing is applying the matching method, and I explained what that is, through several data sources, in this case the census and the voters list. In this case you identified the same person in both sources. And I mentioned that if the JMBGs were correct, it would not have been a problem, but those numbers do not exist, and that forces the Prosecution expert to produce a matching key, and this matching key, it would be only logical to do it in such a way that you have at least a modicum of security that this is the same -- one and the same person, the one that you declared is matched. The matching key should, in addition from guaranteeing this minimum level of assurance that the identified person is one and the same, should remain the same throughout the matching process. What is the matching key for the Prosecution expert is something that we don't really know with that much accuracy, but in the demographic unit of the OTP it is possible to apply 71 keys. In other words, you can change one of the elements 71 times in order to identify a person. It is only in one case that the expert notes that she used the first name, the second name, the ID card number, and the date of birth, and under such criteria, since the ID card number is not listed in any documents, no matches could be obtained. So we can take as our starting point that the expert -- the Prosecution expert uses at the first step, when she says the first step, that means that there is a second step in the matching, and that's an alarm light. There are no steps in the matching process. If you have a good matching key then you have a guarantee that there will be matches. And let me just note that we use the matching method in our everyday lives. You have the cash card that you use to extract money from the cash machine, and you have the pin number, 1234, whatever, and when you put the card in, it has a certain series of numbers written there, and if you tap in your PIN, you get the money. If you make one mistake in just one digit, no matching. You do not get the number. And you don't have the possibility to change those digits 71 times. So the only proper matching is when identification is obtained by matching all the elements in a matching key. So the expert uses the first name, the last name, and the date of birth. In light of the problems that the expert speaks herself about the errors in the first and last names and problems with the dates of birth, in the first step the expert is able to achieve a relatively small number of matches or, for instance, to get 25 per cent of matches. The 20 per cent -- we're talking about 20 per cent of matches with a minimum degree of assurance that matches are proper, but the -- this does not fit the expert's purpose. And then she cuts short the matching key and then she says, "I'm not going to use the first name, last name, and date of birth but only the year of birth," and then she achieves the level of matching of, let's say, 50 to 60 per cent. And then the expert can be unhappy with it, and then they may decide to use only the initial of the first name. And you can then apply 71 criteria in this manner. I'm not saying that Dr. Tabeau is using 71 criteria, but we don't know how many criteria she's actually used, and we know that she does have two steps in the matching process. I assume that she's using the first name, the last name, and the year of birth, because as I verified -- or as I controlled the materials I used those identification details and obtained results that were more or less the same as Dr. Ewa Tabeau's. Let me stress that just the first name, just the last name, and just the date of birth or just the year of birth are not minimally reliable information for the matching process. Let me give you an example. This is something that I got from the demographic unit of the OTP. For instance, in the voters list there are 69 Mirsad Halilovics, and in the census there are 87 persons by the name of Mirsad Halilovic, and of them in the voters list 8 are born -- were born in 1965, and in the census 14 of them were born in that year. So you can match a minimum number of 14, but that multiplies, Mirsad Halilovics born in 1965, and then the Prosecution experts call this the visual method, or they like to use the term "conservative method." So you use some other data and you can say well, this Mirsad is from Sarajevo, this Mirsad is from Mostar. So now you have an opportunity to decide whom to accept and whom to consider matched or identified. The moment in the matching process when you decide what to do gives rise to alarm, because regardless of your fairness, your honesty, your striving to obtain scientific truth, that gives you an opportunity to achieve targeted results. It gives you an opportunity to fit the statistics to the framework of your specific research. So -- yeah, I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I shall give you a concrete example. These are very technical issues we are talking about since something is in dispute on the basis of the various expert reports, and in dispute is the expert report provided by the Prosecution. So let's take the case of a Croatian who comes from Kakanj. He has left Kakanj, and he finds himself in Zagreb. He is then registered with the registry office for refugees in Zagreb. I assume that when he registers he will give his JMBG number. This is a Croatian from Kakanj who is a refugee and who has been registered in Zagreb. The expert that is going to look into his case will have - if I'm making a mistake, please correct me - will have the registration that was registered in the registry office, can check whether -- what his age was in 1992, 1993. Let's say he was 30. And he can check that against the electoral roll in Kakanj. He can also check by checking this data with the census list of 1991 in Kakanj if at the time he resided there. Let's assume that he lived there. As this Croatian was born in Kakanj, he is perhaps a Catholic. The expert can then check whether in the registry of the church which the parish priest has, the expert can check and go to the municipality and check whether this person was registered when this person was born in Kakanj. In this case does the expert not have a whole series of files and data whereby he or she could cross-reference the data? And the expert could then draw a conclusion with a hundred per cent certainty based on the example I've just given you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a number of available data sources, but they're not used. I only use what I can find in the census, what has been registered, and I use only what exists on the voters list, and I'm not interested in anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'm not here to separate the good experts from the bad. I am here to understand an issue. Let's take the case of a Swedish demographer. He is being asked to go and check the fate of a particular refugee who comes from Kakanj and who was registered in Zagreb as a refugee. This expert, would he not do what I have just described, i.e., go to the church registry of Kakanj, go to the municipality, go to the registry office of the municipality, check the electoral roll and check the census data? Is that not what an expert would do to avoid any mistakes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This would be the best thing to do, the most correct thing to do. Whether they would do it or not, I don't know. I must repeat this is a very complex tasks which requires a lot of time, but in many cases -- in most of the cases this can be done. It's feasible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what I have described is what would happen in an ideal world, but if I understand you correctly, Mrs. Tabeau did not do this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This would happen in an ideal world and, yes, Mrs. Tabeau did not do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I take it, Professor Radovanovic, that part of your previous lengthy answer dealt also with the second problem that you -- you outlined. You indicated that there were three problems in Ewa Tabeau's report. Do you recall what the second problem was? The first one thing the methodological incongruent data sources. Then you talked about the second --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The second problem is the modification of matching method which I tried to explain. And the third problem is -- is calculation of non-demographic parameters and proposing the non-demographic parameters as something on which one can draw conclusions on statistical and demographic phenomena. When I say non-demographic parameters I'm saying the following: Dr. Tabeau, for example, discusses the changes in the ethnic structure and mentions certain figures or relative figures. I could open her report and read from it, but let me try and give them an approximation in order to explain. For example, she says that a number of Croats in the territory of the eight municipalities that she considers parts of Herceg-Bosna increased -- was increased by 22 per cent during the period from 1991 to 1997 or 1998, and she derives that information based on the conclusion of the percentage -- changes of the percentage that was calculated in the following way: If the share of Croats in 1991 was, for example, 44 per cent and the share of Croats in 1997 or 1998 according to her estimate of the number of population of that ethnic group is 50-something per cent, Dr. Tabeau derives her conclusion according to which the number of 52.4 per cent in comparison with the percentage of 44.2 is 20 per cent higher. And the calculation is correct. However, it has nothing to do with the increase in the shares of certain ethnicities in the overall population. If there were 44 per cent at one point and now it is 54 per cent, then the increase is only 10 per cent, not more, not 20 or 22 per cent. These are the parameters which are not statistical or demographic. And based on these parameters the OTP experts highlights some things and makes her conclusion on those parameters. To be truthful, the expert also provides a number of tables containing true and correct parameters but she does not provide any comments to them or practically none. There are other problems, for example, comparing apples and oranges within --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. Before it gets lost, I -- I could not quite follow your mathematics. You say if the share, and this is page 52, line 25, if the share of Croats in 1991 was, for example, 44 per cent, and the share of Croats in 1997 or 1998 is 50-something, 54 I think it was first, yes, 54, 44 and then 54 per cent, you say the increase was only 10 per cent. For me the increase is 20 per cent. I don't know how you calculate it, because the increase in -- in numbers is 10, and 10 to 44 is almost 25. Certainly 20 and not 10 per cent, but maybe I'm completely wrong and then I stand to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do my best. A share is the share of Croats in the overall population in 1991, and this is a statistical and demographic parameter. And now we say in 1991, of all the population that resided in the area there were 44.4 Croats, for example. And now we have another statistical parameter that applies to the year 1997 or 1998. We do our calculation and we say that of all the population in 1997 or 1998 resided in the relevant territory, the share of Croats was 54.4 per cent. The share, in comparison with the year 1991, the share in 1997 went up about 10 per cent, and this relative figure at this moment has nothing whatsoever with the total number of population. These are just relative parameters which demonstrate the quality. However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You do not have to go on. The passage which I quoted, you spoke of increase, or it is written "increase," and now you take the percentage, the total percentage, not the increase, and that's of course a different matter. So we must probably correct one or the other. The increase is based on the lower figure, and then there is a certain percentage of increase, and if it's 25 per cent increase it's 25 per cent increase. You say -- or you speak of the increase between 54 up to -- 44 up to 54 of the whole, and that is a different calculation. Then it's 10 per cent. I understand now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, now as far as the ratio is concerned, I listened very carefully to what you have just told us, which was clarified by the question put by my colleague, but here again I think there is a problem which I shall explain to you. If the ratio represents the total number of Croats in the population at the time, you say 42.4 per cent. Let's assume that that is the correct figure. But in 1998 the ratio, i.e., the number of Croatians accounted for in the entire population since there have been a lot of displaced people, a lot of people who have left, who have gone abroad, who have been displaced, some remained in Croatia and so on, in that case I think we shall be comparing apples and oranges, because the basis for the comparison is no longer the same.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To assist both myself and you, please could you look at Table 1 in my report. I don't want to improvise, and I would like to explain what a share is. Technically we're comparing apples and oranges, but this is another methodological issue, and Dr. Tabeau derives another group based on ethnicity and we're again talking about matching. And now we're talking about the meaning of that statistical group. If we accept or if we agree to the fact that by matching data, irrespective of their quality and reliability, Dr. Tabeau arrived at 118-something thousand people in 1987 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. On what page of your report is your table?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In B/C/S it is page 8. I don't know what page would that be in English, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at the B/C/S version. Yes. We are very familiar with this language now. We'll be able to work on this document in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's 9 in English, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This data was taken from Dr. Tabeau's report, and this data shows the collective ethnic structure in the eight municipalities of Herceg-Bosna. In 1991, we can see the total number of adults who were distributed across ethnic groups, and the total number is 231.610. And these are the shares: In the total population Croats accounted for 44.4, Muslims accounted for 34.6, and then follows Serbs and others. The second part refers to the data from 1997, and this is the fruit of Dr. Tabeau's methodology. She compared the census which contains data on ethnicity and electoral rolls which do not contain data on ethnicity. Dr. Tabeau says, "I came up with 118.798 citizens, and when I take their ethnicity as they declared themselves in 1991, this is what their ethnic distribution looks like, so many Croats, so many Muslims, so many Serbs and others." This means she took over the ethnic affiliation from 1991 by the exercise of modify matching in 1997 and 1998, this is the picture that we end up with. Let's not say that the comparison between 1991 and 1997 is good only if they are properly matched. If we calculate all the demographic indicators, we deal with a methodology which says a share of population in the overall population is expressed in percentages and is calculated in the following way, this or the other. And then we see that the share population by ethnicity in 1991 was what it was, whereas in 1997 it was again what it was in 1997. And if we take, for example, Croats for easier calculation, then we can see that the number of Croats who made up the total population in 1991 was 44.4 per cent, which means a share in the total mass of Croats was 44.4 per cent. In 1997, of the total mass of the population that we had at the time, Croats accounted for 55.4 per cent. The conclusion would be that a share of Croats in 1997 and 1998 in comparison with 1991 was up by 10 per cent. The relative indicators give us an opportunity to compare things without going into any absolute figures. What does that mean? Obviously the number is decreasing, the absolute number. However, in order for you to be able to provide a quality explanation of certain things, you use a relative indicator. The fact is that the numbers went down, and nobody's denying that fact. However, if you look at the statistical figures and masses, they do not have the quality changes. They only show quantity changes that apply across the board to all ethnic groups. However, the quality in ethnic terms of that share of population is what is here, and that's why we have an index and a rank here. Indices show how much the share of population went down in a certain period, whereas rank --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Professor Radovanovic. I would like to ask you, you have said the beginning of at least a few minutes ago that the relative indicators give us an opportunity to compare things without going into any absolute figures. What does that mean? "Obviously the number is decreasing, the absolute number," and here I stop at the end of quotation. Now, I really do not see to which number do you refer to when you speak about -- when you mentioned that "obviously the number is decreasing." Do you mean the number of Croats or the number of Muslims or number of whoever? And I would like you to explain, if you would be so kind, to which number and to which population you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, the total number of population is down as well as each ethnic group which constitutes the total number of the population. However, in order to be even more clear, when I said that it was important to put things in perspective and look at relative figures, it is important but it is also important to look at absolute figures. However, when we're talking about the quality of something, if we only have absolute figures then we cannot exercise any quality comparison in matching. Maybe I would be more clear if I said this: In Bosnia-Herzegovina, the birth figure is about 50.000 babies every year. In China the figure is about 7.5 million. Is the birth rate the same in Bosnia and China? What would you say? At a first glance it's absolutely impossible if you compare 50.000 with 7.5 million. That is why we have the relevant statistical and demographic indicators which give us the birth rate. I'm again speaking off my head. I'm saying that the birth rate in Bosnia is, for example, 13 per mil, whereas the birth rate in China is also 13 per mil. And now I have a quality indicator which says that the birth rate of China and Bosnia do not differ at all. However, I know the quality and the frequency of birth, the rate tells us that 13 new babies are born per 1.000 inhabitants. Bosnia has population that it has, China has the number that it has, and per each thousand new -- 13 new babies are born. This gives me the frequency and the quality of something. And in those terms the relative indicators or shares speak about the quality, not about the quantity of something. The quantity changed, but there is no quality changes in the structure of the population when it comes to Croats and Muslims. There is quality change which applies across the board. It applies to Croats, Muslims, Serbs, and others equally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you for this explanation. On the other hand, I have to confess that I'm still not very much convinced. Then you say, "The quantity changes but there is no quality changes in the structure of the population when this comes to Croats and Muslims," it is a quotation what you have just said. Then I really do not see the basis of this statement because there were at least 10 per cent increase of the numbers of Croats, if I'm not mistaken, from 44 to 54-something. So it is what I am trying to -- getting at, that what is the -- what is your figures about the changes in general among the three major contingents of the population in -- at least in Herzegovina at that time, that is the Croats, the Bosniaks, and the Serbs? So it is what I would like you to point out. And frankly, I'm not very much convinced with the comparison with the Chinese birth rate, because you know that it is a quite other issue. And I would like you to -- again to come back to the original question, and that is the changes in the overall picture of population in that particular area, that is among the three major groups. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The data we are looking at is not my data. This is the OTP expert's data. The OTP expert claims that the number of Croats in 1997, in comparison with the year 1991, went up by -- actually the percentage of Croats went up by 22 per cent. I'm saying no to this. Taking into account the OTP Prosecutor's data and applying the correct methodology of shares and not the percentual [as interpreted] estimate of percentages, and this gives me a different picture, a picture that shows that the figure -- the number did change but the percentage did not go up by 20 -- the share of Croats did not go up by 22 per cent. It only went up by less than 10 per cent. I have tried, but I don't seem to have been clear, to explain how the non-statistical demographic indicators were used by the expert to claim something that is incorrect and how it would look if the expert used a proper statistical and demographic indicator. And I'm quoting this, and I'm providing my explanation for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I look at the table, one notices that there is a share of 44.4 moving to 54.2, and Muslims move from 44.6 to 37.4, and therefore a logical mind would deduce that now -- by now, by 1997 there were many more Croats than there were in 1991. Well, that is an assessment or a conclusion that one can draw. Now, if I make the following analysis, as you were speaking I did the subtraction between the number of Croats in 1997 and the Croats from 1991, and when you do that subtraction, you realise that there's a deficit of 38.499 Croats. As I subtract the number of Muslims from 1997 to 1991 -- or 1991 to 1997, rather, there's about 36.000 Croats -- sorry, Muslims -- fewer Muslims. Now, that difference, if I look at the population from 1991, 100 and so many thousands and 80-something thousand for the Muslims. Now if I for the number of Croats have gone down by 38.499 down from 102.866, it's about 44 per cent and if I do the same calculation with the Muslims, I also end up at 44 per cent, and therefore a logical mind may deduce that there hasn't been a significant change. What do you think about that, since I have 44 per cent in both cases?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under the assumption that you are happy and that you accept the figure that Dr. Tabeau claims as the number of identified person there, if we accept that identification, and we will see that she first says there was a certain number and then she changes that to 80.000. She operates with three different figures. And if we are to deduce apples from oranges we can end up with that figure, but I simply deny the methodology used by Dr. Tabeau, and I believe that this is not a good number. It could be either higher or lower, but Dr. Tabeau also is not certain. She says one thing at one time and another thing at a different time. The 170.000 [as interpreted] inhabitants in a table of this sort in this type of calculation represents the constant population of the eight municipalities at the moment when they voted, and that's the only way they could be compared with 230.000. And although she provides that in the first table, Dr. Tabeau goes on to claim that the number of permanent inhabitants who resided there in 1991 and voted in 1997 were no more than 80.000. And then when we come to the matching exercise, she reduces the 80.000 and ends up with 64.000 refugees. And if we accept all the figures provided by Dr. Tabeau, then your conclusion is absolutely correct. This is nothing more than a simple mathematical operation which demonstrates precisely what you have just told us. If we accept statistical and demographic indicators, however, which were derived based on the same data, they also show that there is no radical change at all. The ranks of the representation of certain ethnic groups, especially Muslims and Croats, have remained the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Karnavas. It's just a matter of probably of either translation or recording. I'm referring to two lines, the last of page 56, and 57 the first two lines. I read what the expert is referred as having said: "And then we see that the share population by ethnicity in 1991 was what it was, whereas in 1997 it was again what it was in 1997." To me this is a total tautology and I don't know whether you said this or whether you wanted to say something with some content.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The share in 1997 is as is indicated in the table. That's what I wanted to say, because I didn't want to go through the exercise of reading each and every percentage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, thank you. That's different. If you wanted to say it's what's in the table, that's a different matter, but when you say 1997 it was what it was in 1997, that is a zero sentence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Maybe I could -- I don't want to dwell on this table because we have some other matters to cover, but these figures that are listed in 1991 column and 1997 column, okay, the total and then the breakdown, Croats, Muslim, Serb and others, how reliable are these figures for 1991? Let's start with that. How reliable are they?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The data were taken over from the census, but the Prosecution expert took persons in certain age brackets as adults in 1997 in order to have comparable data. It's relatively reliable. Why do I say relatively reliable? It's not because I doubt in the population figures as presented in the census, but purely methodologically there is a method for putting together the age brackets. Dr. Tabeau said "all those who were born in 1980 and before, I declare them to be legal adults because that means that in 1998 they would be eligible to vote." And generally speaking now, I don't want to go into that, but Dr. Tabeau does not say whether this is the calendar year, the year of birth or whatever, but let us now agree to accept that. There is another problem that is rather controversial here. If you put together this set that you want to compare with 1997, and we're not going into the quality now, the datum from 1991, if you aged, if I may say so, a certain percentage of the people, don't you take into account that some of them may have died in the meantime or moved out. In 1997 -- well, I can't tell you now. I have this information here in the hotel. I think there were some 10.000 people for all those municipalities that were above 75 years of age. Technically speaking, they are potential voters. You have the vital statistics indicating that in the eight municipalities, 1996, 1997, 1998, over 5.000 people died. What about those who died in 1992, 1993, 1994, 1995? Official statistics do not provide us with the data. The demographic unit does have, on the special order of the Tribunal in The Hague, the statistics of the federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and of Republika Srpska, the institutes or the bureaus did a special research or study into the mortality between 1992 and 1995. Those databases exist in the demographic unit of the Prosecution. If it is possible to match those with the voters list in order to take the ethnic background of a person and glue it onto the -- onto a voter, then it would be only fair to clean up the 1991 census using the same methodology and to trim it down to a more acceptable level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I'm sorry to interrupt. It's just if I could have a page cite on this issue of deaths from the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That can be covered on cross-examination at this point in time, unless we want to take a break and the expert can look at it at this point in time, but as I understand it my colleague is not going to be cross-examining for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, I'm looking at your table, and that will be the last question before the break, table number 1. I'm looking at the situation regarding Serbs. 30.495 in 1991. In 1997 there were only 3.281 left. So, you know, all -- most of them have disappeared. And in terms of the rank, actually, they ranked number 4. So when we talk about ethnic cleansing at the time is the first ethnic group concerned, wouldn't it be the Serbians? The Serbs, sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a demographer. I don't know what ethnic cleansing is. I know what changes in the ethnic structure are. These data indicate that the most radical changes within the ethnic groups that we considered were experienced by others, and they include Yugoslavs and some other ethnic communities and by Serbs. But I stress once again this -- these are not my data. These are data taken from Dr. Ewa Tabeau's report, and I indicate the source here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. And so if we understand things correctly, in the index the Croats and Muslims retain the same rank as indicated by Mrs. Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. According to these data, they have the same rank, and qualitatively speaking, there are no major changes. Serbs and others experience radical downsizing, and this is what can be seen from Dr. Ewa Tabeau's table. But this is not the conclusion that she draws. Dr. Tabeau reaches a completely different conclusion. She talks about Croats specifically, Muslims specifically. She uses a term that is unheard-of in demographics, and that's non-Croats. I may understand that it might be used in some areas but not in demographics. What is a non-Croat? All those who are not Croats. And who is a non-Serb? So Dr. Tabeau does not provide us with an analytical table which would then, regardless of whether I agree or disagree with her data, even the data obtained in this manner would then show that in relation to Croats and Muslims there are no radical changes. There are no radical changes of the ethnic structure. Dr. Tabeau provides us with a huge pile of simple tables, and there is a major difference between analytical tables and simple tables, where she shows each ethnic group separately. It is very difficult to find one's way around all that. I wanted to say that the results obtained by Dr. Tabeau and her conclusions are not consistent when we're talking about ethnic structure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, ma'am, on the table we have -- I think that it would have been useful to have the previous census figures dating back from 1981. Do you have the figures of the total population from 1981 with a breakdown of Croats, Muslims, and Serbs to see whether from 1981 until 1991 there was or wasn't a decrease due to the fact that some have moved to the West or have gone on to work in Germany, et cetera? Do you have these figures with you or don't you have them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have the figures. Not here but in the witness room. I have a book published by the Federal Institute, by ethnic composition and it provides the ethnic structure at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the 1948 census up to 1991 census. I wanted to draw your attention to this fact. The Federal Institute publishes data for the overall population and Dr. Tabeau here represents only the adult population. But if we look at the overall population for that level we can see that there are no radical changes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if you can have a look at this book during the break and tell me how many was the total population in 1981, how many Croats and Muslims, I think it could be useful. Okay. We're going to take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Witness, during the break you were able to have a look at your book. Can you tell us what the population figures were in 1981 and what the breakdown was between the Croats, the Serbs, and the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the book published by the Federal Institute For Population Statistics. It was done in Zagreb, this book, but it pertains to the 1991 census. At page 1 of this book we have a comparative overview of population in Bosnia and Herzegovina for the censuses between 1990 -- 1948 to 1991 providing a broader range of ethnic groups. In 1981, there were 4.124.256 inhabitants. Out of this figure 758.140 inhabitants were Croats. I have to consult this piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Perhaps we could put it on the ELMO so that way, everyone can see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So 758.146 Croats; 1.630.033 Muslims; 1.320.738 Serbs; and here we have all the other ethnic groups where the Yugoslavs were the largest group, 326.316 inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, in the table at the bottom we see the percentage figures in 1991, 17.4 per cent of Croats, 17.4, and 43.5 of Muslims, 30.1 -- 31.2 Serbs. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't have the table, however, for the eight municipalities. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In this book we don't have the tables for the eight localities, but we have something else. We have the cantons in Bosnia projecting the figures for 2002, and here we can have a breakdown by municipality. We can have the -- it's the assessment for the number of inhabitants in Bosnia and Herzegovina ethnicity by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did Your Honour want to look at -- see that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, if you feel it is useful to have the figures for 2002 for the eight cantons --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I was just asking, Your Honours, given that my time is limited and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me go back to one of the -- one of the things that you said, because there were lots of questions concerning these numbers in the table that you showed, and I did ask you a question about how reliable they were, but at one point you began by saying that the ethnic affiliation by modified matching, Ewa Tabeau used this method, ethnic -- I take it identifying ethnic affiliation by modified matching. Can you please explain what you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In voters lists there is no information about the ethnic background or ethnic affiliation. In order to obtain the information about the ethnic affiliation of the persons who registered as voters, the Prosecution expert did the matching. And I've already told you how she modified the key, first name, last name, year of birth. And when she matched a person, she states she is able to obtain the information about the ethnic background from the census whether this person is a Muslim, Croat, Serb, Yugoslav. And then she adopts the ethnic background and glues it onto the information from the voters list and says, "In accordance with my matched data, these voters are of this ethnic background." And she presents this as two completely separate and independent data sources, and now you compare what the situation was like in 1991 with what was going on in 1997. This is not correct. Technically and practically you're comparing what was going on in 1991 with again what was going on in 1991 for the persons that you managed to match. What is the big problem here? In all the censuses in the former Yugoslavia, the criterion for the declaration of one's ethnic background was subjective. It's a subjective criterion, and that means that I can decide at any given moment, based on how I'm feeling, having assessed the political situation, having taken a dislike to the census-taker, I can decide at one census to declare myself as a Serb, at the second census to declare myself as a Croat or as a Yugoslav, and I also had the right not to declare my ethnic background. So it is a subjective criterion which gives you an opportunity to change your declaration of your ethnic affiliation. And I am sure that there were cases of this kind, and in some ethnic groups in some ethnic communities which are smaller, and if you have a smaller mass in statistics it is more sensitive and all the problems are more visible. In smaller ethnic groups you can see the huge irregularities cropping up from one census to the next. And these irregularities cannot be explained away in demographic terms. They are simply a consequence of people declaring themselves differently. And it is quite interesting for us to look at this category Yugoslavs here. Given the political climate at the time when the census is taken in 1991, the political unrest, the imminent break-up of Yugoslavia, you can see that the number of Yugoslavs has gone down substantially. I think that a rough calculation would be a decrease of about 100.000 Yugoslavs less in the ten years between 1981 and 1991. It cannot be explained by demographics, because Yugoslavs did not move out in such great numbers, and they did not die in such great numbers. So the only way in which you can explain that is that they declared themselves differently. And since we now have in front of us the information ranging from 1948 to 1991, it is interesting to look at the number of Muslims, and we can see a growth that cannot be explained in terms of demographics. You can see that in 1961, you can see that there were 842.248 Muslims, and we can see that in 1991 the number was 1.484.430 Muslims. It is a substantial increase in the number of people who declare themselves as Muslims. It was not a case of 500.000 Muslims moving in from other areas or the population growth being that high. So such drastic changes can be explained by the fact that the people declared themselves differently. I am giving you Muslims as an example here. This is quite complex in light of the fact that from one census to the next the options for declaring ethnic affiliation differed, and this is a good example because it is rather drastic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just a question. Ms. Radovanovic, is there any other way than self-declaration to fix the ethnic identity of a person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the census.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And is the census based on self-declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, exclusively on that, on self-declaration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So in fact there is no other way than asking a person to know whether that person is a Muslim or a Croat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What about the voter registration list? Didn't they list the national make-up of the individual?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. Nobody asked people to declare their ethnicity. At that moment this was not considered significant. Your ethnicity did not matter. I repeat, the voter registration list does not contain the question on ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The increase between 1961 and 1991 in the number of Muslims, 500.000, that is a very high figure. What is that due to? Is it due to the birth rate or is it due to other factors, i.e., that the Muslims in 1961 felt they had no identity, were not recognised as such and it is only in 1991 when one talks about a possible independence that there is an awareness about this? How can you explain such a differential over a period of 30 years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a problem in statistical terms, and it is as follows: In the 1948 census, there was a possibility for anybody to declare themselves as a person without ethnicity or a Muslim Serb, a Muslim Croat, a Muslim Macedonian and so on and so forth. In the 1953 census, the statistical nomenclature included a determinant which says a Muslim in ethnic rather than in religious sense. The 1961 census says Muslim as nationality, i.e., national affiliation. That's how it was described. The 1971 census says Muslim with a capital M, which denotes affiliation with a certain people. And that continued in 1981, 1991. And most probably it will be the same in 2011 in Bosnia. And I suppose this will change into Bosniak. In statistical and demographic sense this data show a broad range not only because of the natural population growth. I believe that this includes one part of natural growth. Primarily it is due to the ethnic consolidation, i.e., the way people declared themselves and the way they were instructed to declare themselves from one census to the next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you think the religious factor may have played a part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure. I would not be able to define it that way. There is a confusion here that was created by the State of Yugoslavia. Nowhere in the world will you find the determinant Muslim as national or ethnic affiliation. This is a religious determinant, a confessional determinant. I don't believe that the ethnic factor played a decisive role, but I never studied that, and I would not be able to tell you whether it did play a role or not in all that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, this increase, 500.000 people, was this not due to the fact that the central -- the federal government did not play a part in this and let people express their faiths, which means that some people claimed to belong to the Muslim faith as a result of this, because the Communist regime was lagging behind in these matters, or was it due to something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We lived in a very specific system which believed that it had solved the national issue in the best possible way, and I believe that this could have reflected the freedoms that existed. You could declare yourself to be whatever you wanted to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'd like to get back to this issue of the increase in the number of Muslims between 1948 and 1991 through the various census, and you said that each person declared he or she belonged to a particular ethnicity. I was a little bit surprised by that, because in a socialist [Realtime transcript read in error nationalist"] Yugoslavia this system along ethnic lines had been designed to balance things out. Now, if people could change ethnicity from one census to another, how could the State clearly establish the nationality of a particular person and then conflicts could erupt in the case, for instance, when positions needed to be shared out between the various ethnicities. When some positions had been earmarked for Serbs or Croats and then one person could just change his or her nationality, his or her ethnicity and state that he or she had a different nationality as opposed to what had been stated in the previous census, what happened then? I'm sorry. Judge Prandler has remarked that on page 73, line 20 it says nationalist Yugoslavia. No. I talked about socialist Yugoslavia. Now, could you answer my question, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your question is rather complex and entails a few things that I may not be an expert in. In a political sense we lived in a state where there was fraternity and unity, and nobody had the need to emphasise their nationality. On the other hand, yes, there was a key when positions were allocated to have all the nationalities represented. However, a census allowed you to declare yourself the way you wanted. The -- a census was not a benchmark for somebody to look at the census and see whether Svetlana Radovanovic declared herself a Serb in 1981 and then as a Croat in 1991. The political circles had their own keys to do stuff, and that's as much as I know. You even have a clause for the 1991, 1981, and 1971 census which says under the constitution anybody has the right not to declare their ethnic background. So nobody was forced to declare themselves in those terms. However, the atmosphere, primarily political atmosphere of a census, in an ethnically heterogeneous midst and the interviewer whose influence can also be felt and can be of a decisive role, all this contributed to people not answering questions which were not precisely defined, which could be considered as subjective. Those issues were disputable. Those questions were disputable. When I say disputable, I'm not trying to deny the statistical official data of the Bosnia-Herzegovina statistics. What I'm saying is that an expert, a demographer who is looking at the national breakdown can use official data to do so, but they have to have good knowledge of methodology and the times and the ways the data was collected. And also such an expert has to be very cautious. They have to tread with caution, because we're talking about the way people declared themselves. The way I declare my national position, my ethnic position in technical terms, does not have to do any -- anything to do with my national identity proper. In the census I can say that I hail from Papua, new -- that's my right. In cultural terms my national identity can also be my private matter, and I don't have to declare myself as anything should I not wish to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me -- let me just ask you a simple question, and I'm going to ask you to give me shorter answers. I don't have unlimited time, regrettably, so -- but essentially the question is this: How reliable is this report that we have been speaking of? How reliable are the data, the statistics? To what extent within the scientific community of demography would this sort of report, the methods that were used, the data that was collected, the manner in it was processed, how reliable is it?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This report does not meet even the minimum requirement of reliability. It is a product of methodologically incongruent sources of data which abound in mistakes and by the application of modified standard methods that were used in statistics and demographics. And in those terms the report cannot be qualified either as either an expert report or a scientific report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, in her testimony Dr. Tabeau at some point indicated that this was sort of a unique technique or a unique method being use here in demography. And perhaps -- and I know that you listened -- you listened to her testimony. Can you please explain to us whether this methodology is unique and, if so, where -- how reliable is it as a methodology within the demographic field?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is not a scientific or professional methodology. It is unique, and it is applied and used only in the demographic department of The Hague department and nowhere else in the world as far as I know. And I believe that I'm familiar with quite a lot of literature produced all over the world and in the former Yugoslavia. There is no single expert or scientific research that has used a method modified in this way or similar data sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now we're going to speak briefly about the second report, but perhaps given your answer, it begs the question how then, given the way you have criticised Brunborg and Tabeau, how is it that they are using this methodology, if we want to call it that? Is it that they don't know? Is it that they're on the cutting edge? Is it that you might be wrong?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, doesn't that really call for speculation? How is the expert to know what was in the minds of Dr. Tabeau?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Here's -- I can answer that, and this is why I don't think it's speculation, because we're dealing with an expert and so if an expert, for instance, manipulates data, manipulates sources, and it would appear from the testimony, and I'll put the question if this is manipulation going on, then obviously we may be getting closer to the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you expecting an answer from me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll back up. I'll rephrase for the benefit of the Bench. Is manipulation going on and, if so, please inform the Trial Chamber how is it that these experts would be manipulating data sources, methodology?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is manipulation. Why do I dare qualify it as such? I do, because I believe that the OTP expert knows exactly what correct methods are, how they are applied, what are good sources of data. If I had never participated in drafting any report, the expert did not have to read any of my reports, she would still know what I'm talking about. She's a demographer. She's qualified. She has educational -- certain educational background, and she has certain knowledge in demographics. If I have read six reports drafted by the OTP expert and all the six refer to different areas, to different municipalities, to different ethnic groups and different accused, and all six of them are based on the same sources of data, which was the 1991 census and the lists of voters, they all use the same modified matching method. They all match non-existent ethnic structures. They all deal with refugees and displaced persons by simple deduction of the number of population in 1991 and what the expert matched. They all say we have a statistical definition of refugees and displaced person. There is no such definition, and any demographer is aware of that -- aware of that. What I'm saying is that if they're absolutely identical, if they use the same sources, if they use the same methodology, then I would be confident to say that they are all a product of manipulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you see -- do you see any efforts in -- as far as the numbers, generating numbers, percentages or high numbers as part of this manipulative process and, if so, could you please explain how such manipulation may or indeed be going on by this particular unit of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that the expert strived to augment the numbers of certain groups of population. If she needed more refugees and displaced persons, she could manipulate and say, "This is as many as I matched." There was always an evident strive towards augmentation, and this was based on what the expert's brief was as to what she was supposed to find. And as for matching, for example, if you use in one case 71 criteria to match one thing with another, this is already dubious, but in this particular case and in these reports, the expert says, "I'm using a matching method." She says, "I have two steps to do so." And she does not give us the statistics of the steps. This means that the expert is covering up and prevents us from looking at the degree of combinations that she's using. When I say statistics, this is what I mean: The witness says, "I've matched 140.000 people from the voting lists to the census," but she doesn't say that she did that according to the criteria of name, family name, the name of the father, the date of birth, 20 per cent; according to the criteria of name, the family name, the date of birth, 50 per cent, and so on and so forth. Another criteria would be just the initials without the whole name and the figure would be 80 per cent. And this matching statistics would give us a true representation of the combinations that the expert was using, and we would also have the right, the true picture of the group of data that had a certain degree of reliability. The expert knows how to do the statistics. She's the one that does the data. In no single report have I seen the matching statistics that I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go on to the second report. This is P 09837. This is the report that you had an opportunity to also look at; is that correct? It's at the very end.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And here we can see from the title, "Killed persons related to the siege of Mostar." In demographics could you please define what "siege" means in your field, in your science of demography?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't define this because the term "siege" does not exist in demography.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is it the demographer's job to characterise an event as a siege, for instance?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is not a task of a demographer, because they don't have any expertise to do that. I believe that it would be the military, the politics, or some other area that would deal with that. But a demographer might venture to do so. However, if they want to venture into somebody else's area in scientific terms, then it would be professionally fair and correct for them to put a footnote and explain their understanding of the term "siege."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Very briefly if you could tell us, having analysed this report, did you find any problems with it and, if so, if you could just briefly describe them to us.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, problems are primarily methodological in nature, and they boil down to the data sources and to the manner and method applied by the Prosecution expert. Manipulating the figures are also quite obvious, but something that really astonished me is the construction of two new methods for the determination of the ethnic background. I have never seen this anywhere except in the demographic unit of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Could you please explain that, and I will ask you to speak slower, okay, because you're using some technical terms. It's getting late, and this is obviously rather important since we seem to be sort of ploughing through uncharted territory.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The expert uses two data sources. The first data source is the registry books, the register of deaths. The second data source are the registry books of the War Hospital. The first data source --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can you please tell us how much time we have left. Please proceed, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I did, Your Honour, have approximately 48 minutes coming into the court after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you could pick it up from the top.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct. The Registrar's going to let us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Go ahead, because you're eating into my time now because of that interruption, if you could go ahead and please answer the question, specifically about the manipulation in this particular report.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The first data source are the registers of birth [as interpreted], which are a statistical source of data, but they do not contain information about the ethnic background; yet the expert draws conclusions about the ethnic background from this source. The second source is the registry book of the War Hospital. It is an amateurish source, not done in accordance with any statistical methodology. It does not contain any information about the ethnic background but the Prosecution expert has a way of dealing with that. The third important methodological problem is that the expert does not know what East Mostar is; yet all the time she keeps talking about East Mostar she is unable to define the area that she's studying. And in conceptual -- the conceptual, temporal, and spatial coverage of what you're studying is an important methodological element. So that would be it in a nutshell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's go back. If we can go to the second one, at least, where you indicated that she has a way of dealing with the -- I believe it was the ethnic background, and that dealt with the -- with the book. You indicated that there were three problems, madam, so I'm looking at the second problem that you indicated, and you said that Ewa Tabeau has no problem in making determinations on the ethnic background. Could you please explain what you mean.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The expert uses two methods, and I have to say "methods." One has to do with the determination of the ethnic structure based on the register of deaths, and the second has to do with the determination of the ethnic structure based on the books from the War Hospital. The ethnic structure, on the basis of the books from the War Hospital, is based -- is done with the assistance of experts. She does not state what educational background those experts have, who they are. On the basis of the first name and the last name. And as for the ethnic structure, based on the register of deaths she determines it on the basis of the frequency of the appearance of a certain name in the censuses, and on the basis of the frequency she determines what ethnic background the dead person has. What this means is if the name Svetlana has a higher frequency among Croats than among Serbs, then Svetlana is a Croat. If the name Svetlana appears with greater frequency among Serbs than among Croats or Muslims, then Svetlana is a Serb. As far as I'm concerned, that was rather astonishing, and I have yet to see or hear of another case when it was done in this manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How reliable are the results in this particular report? And when I say "reliable," I'm speaking about it within the scientific community of demography.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: They are absolutely unreliable. If we take into account only the way in which the ethnic structure was determined, if we look at the quality of the sources, then we cannot accept them. And in particular if we take into account the fact that you don't know what area is covered, if you cannot define something, then how can we talk about any reliability? It is absolutely unreliable. And the fact that speaks to it in particular is the fact that there is not a single piece of information that is vital for demographers telling us what segment of the population are we talking about when we talk about those registered as dead. Is it 0.5 per cent, 15 per cent, 50 per cent? It is absolutely impossible to divine that, because we don't know area is covered and what population is covered. And this analysis is not an analysis at all, because it is not labelled an analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is labelled the siege of Mostar. Could you please assist me. I don't have it in front of me. "Persons killed in the siege of Mostar, statistical analysis of the books of the Mostar War Hospital and the Mostar registers of death."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you this: Have you ever seen this methodology applied within the field of demographics?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Did you see any manipulation in this particular report in order to augment a particular ethnic group and, if so, how?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I did see instances of that, and it would be simpler to actually show where. Although Dr. Ewa Tabeau does not know what East Mostar is, she has table 12 in her report where she presents the criteria --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's page 15, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, continue.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let me find it. That's table 12, I believe. I can't find it now. Yes. Table 12. "An overview of the criteria for the selection of data for the analysis of deaths related to the siege of Mostar." And I would like you to pay attention to line 1. In the last column we see the figure 539. There is the result that the Prosecution exert --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me. I'm sorry to interrupt. It's table 12 of which report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It's page 15 in the English version, page 15.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's P 09837. That's the second report that we've been discussing for the last 20 minutes, and we're on page 15. This is table 12 under paragraph number 4.1, the selection procedure summarising table 12. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So continue, Professor.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Here we have 539 cases, and here you have the criteria, how this was obtained. In the first line it says number, validity, duplicate, what material is it. And then it says "East Mostar." Whether it is or it is not East Mostar, and it says "No." And then whether the year corresponds, yes, whether this was war-related cause, yes, and then whether you have surname, first name, and so on. Dr. Tabeau also notes this in the text, not only in the table, and she says -- should I now find it to quote, because I don't want to paraphrase. At page 6 of the Serbian version, the version in B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you give us the -- the number of the paragraph? That would help us.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: They should be numbered, like 2.2, 2.3.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Or page 4, page 4 in English. Okay. It's page 4.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I can't find it. Okay. Okay. Dr. Tabeau says this: "Although the category 'Not East Mostar' mainly refers to the records of deaths from outside East Mostar, the records from East Mostar which for various reasons have not been marked as East Mostar are contained under this category as well."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Anything else that you wish to comment in particular to this -- this report as far as the problems, manipulations, anything that would assist the Trial Chamber in its evaluation of it? You don't --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, something that is called a distribution method that Dr. Tabeau uses, she uses in both reports, but in this report this is particularly pronounced. The data distribution method exists in statistics, and this is not something that is controversial, but it is a recommendation, at least when it comes to official statistics is not to use it in statistical research. It means that you have a set of statistical units, and one part possesses a certain feature and the other part does not. In this specific case it means that out of, let's say, 400 cases, 4 -- or, rather, out of 439 cases that Dr. Tabeau lists as persons killed because of the siege of Mostar -- and I would like to ask you to look at table 2 from my report, the data were taken from Dr. Tabeau. No, that's the cause of death. No. I didn't give you the right reference. So this relates to 539 cases that are classified in according -- in accordance with the cause of death. In all of those cases you have the cause of death. And you will see that in most of those cases the cause of death is not listed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please repeat the number of cases for which the cause of death was determined.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Slow down. You'll need to repeat yourself, and again, which table are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about table 2 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- from my report or, rather, this is a table that is contained in Dr. Tabeau's report. Maybe it would be clearer if I were to refer to that, the point. So what is the point? So for the overall mass you don't have the cause of death. You have the cause of death for only one part of the mass, and that's 135 cases. And now you classify them. Total shelling, 76 cases killed; 34 cases gunshot wounds and so on. I'm not going into that, whether the cause of death was determined properly or not. Now, in order to be able to show all the cases --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry, the expert is referring to table 16 on page 17 of the Tabeau report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I'm going to have to ask you, madam, because we're trying to make a clear record, you need to make reference to Tabeau's report so we know. Now we know that we're speaking about table 16 in P0 9837, which is on page 17 on the English. Okay. So if you could continue. Just go ahead with your narrative so I can conclude today. This is the distribution of the victims in the siege according to cause of death, this is the table, and it's under 16 in -- it's on 28, page 28 -- okay.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Table 16, distribution of the victims of the siege according to cause of death. You can see here that you have a total of 539 persons that are classified according to their cause of death. Out of that, 404 persons do not have the cause of death determined. Now Dr. Tabeau makes an estimate. You can look at column number 3, estimated cause of death. You see shelling was 76 in the original data sources, and now she extrapolates and estimates that there are 303. How does she make that estimate? For the known group of persons in the known death category, and then we're talking about 76 plus 34, plus 18, plus 6, plus 1. That's 135. Now she says 135 is 100 per cent. 76 of the 135, that would be about 50 per cent. The 50 per cent, now I calculate the 50 per cent of the 404, and it's 200 and something or other. 200 and something plus 76, that's 303 cases. So I estimate that their cause of death was shelling. And she does that for all causes of death. So this method, the distribution method, means that the proportion in a smaller mass is transferred to a larger mass, and you know in advance that you will get bigger figures, because 30 percent of 100 and 30 per cent of 400, it's a huge difference. So this method, the proportion method, it's a well-known method, but applied in this manner to such a small mass it is particularly sensitive because you can see that we get an increase of by three or four times. This method applied to a large statistical mass was used in the census, and let me tell you when it was. A certain number of people did not have their age group determined, and if you have 4.4 million inhabitants of Bosnia and Herzegovina, you did not know there the age of maybe 1 or 3, up to 3 or 4 per cent of them. So in order not to have this information as unknown, then you make a proportionate calculation. But if you have such a small mass you increase the figures by 4 times across the board. So from this point of view, using this method constitutes abuse, because a demographer knows that if you apply it to small statistical mass, your data end up being deformed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I guess I have one final question and that would be with respect to the third report by Ewa Tabeau, recognising that you did not provide a written analysis of that, can you just in one brief sentence tell us whether the same methods are used in that report dealing with the wounded as the ones that you just explained dealing with the dead?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. As Mr. Karnavas has just voiced, there's no written report on this. This is not something that we're prepared to deal with and it should not be asked of this witness, particularly if she has not prepared an expert report about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but on the tables it mentions the injured, so it might be interesting to see how all this was calculated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can you tell us how the injured were calculated based on the President's observation? How does Ewa Tabeau tabulate the injured as opposed to the dead?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what table? What table? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, should the witness not at least be asked whether she has studied this report at all, because that is not -- that should be the foundation for any further question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, the witness has indicated that -- she said this early on, Your Honours, at the very, very beginning, if you go to the beginning of my -- I'll be more than happy to get the page number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to look at the third report?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And in my second report I mentioned the fact that within the War Hospital there were 6.000 wounded, but I studied in great detail the third report, too, and I didn't say --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all the microphones please be switched off that are not in use.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not put it in my report first of all because I didn't have enough time, but the second reason was that would constitute repetition, pure and simple, because all the problems are the same. There's only one data source, the War Hospital books. The area again is unknown, the territory is unknown. The only thing we know is that the War Hospital was on the left bank of the Neretva in eastern part of Mostar. And then we can go on to the way in which various things were calculated, statistics that are her own. And this is again not an analysis. This is simply a comment on the data source from which you extract some statistical data, and if you cannot compare it to anything, then what analysis are we talking about? So if I extract my own data and I present my data, there's no comparation. I'm not putting them in relation to anything. It's not -- it's no analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is there a problem, Judge Trechsel? I mean, we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We wanted -- we wanted to ask the Defence as far as tomorrow is concerned. Who is going to be taking the floor tomorrow? From what I understood, Praljak Defence counsel and Petkovic Defence counsel would like to take the floor. Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours -- Your Honour, I would just like to ask one thing, since to my mind some things that I believe I should be able to clear up with the madam still exist. Is it possible that at the expense of the time that I'm allotted for the cross-examination that we get some more time since the topic is a highly complex one, very important, and it begs for a full clarification so that we can understand what we're talking about. I believe that I can do a good job, and I would like to ask for some time that I have not been allotted in accordance with the rules, an hour and whatever it is that we're -- we get, because I believe that Madam Alaburic will be cross-examining. If I can have some time that then will be deducted from the time that I will be given later. I beg for your understanding, because in light of the incrimination or -- that Mostar was subjected to on selective shelling and that it was under siege, it is very important for me and for General Petkovic to clarify every single detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. General Praljak and I tried to divide the time allotted to us, and it turned out that an hour and a half was not enough to him, and I would like to support his motion that we be allowed to examine this witness slightly longer. We don't believe that it will be longer than an hour and a half so that General Praljak gets about an hour and -- an hour and 10, and I as a modest woman will be happy with 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber had decided it would be an hour, but we shall discuss it again. I have understood that there will be no questions from Stojic and Pusic Defence counsel, from Mr. Coric Defence counsel either; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. President, Your Honours. I can confirm that as matters stand at the moment, there is no intention on behalf of Mr. Stojic to ask this witness any questions at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Coric's Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PLAVEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we won't have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President, you're right. We will not be cross-examining this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber, after having deliberated, decides that for the Petkovic Defence counsel and Praljak Defence counsel will have an hour and a half all in all. You can share the time out as you deem fit. I believe Praljak Defence will need one hour, and Mrs. Alaburic half an hour, but anyway, it's for you to sort it out. Last recommendation, Witness, tomorrow we shall resume at 9.00. Your testimony will be very short tomorrow. Since you are a witness of the Court, you must not contact Mr. Karnavas in any way. This is something I am sure you have been advised of already. You will return tomorrow, and the hearing will start at 9.00. I wish you all a very pleasant evening.
